lesson.title: Asking a String What It Is: isdigit, isalpha, and Friends
lesson.summary: Validation methods like isdigit(), isalpha(), and isspace() let a program check what kind of characters a string contains before trusting or converting it.
lesson.body:
Every string method you have learned so far, like upper(), replace(), or split(), transforms a string into something new or breaks it into pieces. Validation methods do something different: they inspect a string and answer a yes or no question about its content, returning a boolean. This turns out to be essential any time your program receives text from a user or a file and needs to decide, before doing anything risky, whether that text is actually usable.

The most commonly used validation methods are isdigit(), isalpha(), isalnum(), isupper(), islower(), and isspace(). isdigit() returns True only if every character in the string is a digit character, and the string is not empty: "42".isdigit() is True, but "42.5".isdigit() is False, because the period is not a digit, and "".isdigit() is also False, since there are no characters to check at all. isalpha() checks that every character is a letter, so "hello".isalpha() is True while "hello!".isalpha() is False because of the exclamation point. isalnum() is more permissive, accepting any mix of letters and digits, so "room101".isalnum() is True even though neither isalpha() nor isdigit() alone would accept it.

These methods matter because they let you validate input before you try to use it, which connects directly to the string methods you already know: validation methods are called the same way, with dot notation on a string, but instead of producing a new string they produce a fact about the one you have. Consider a program that asks the user for their age. If you write age = int(input("Enter your age: ")) and the user types "twenty", the int() conversion crashes the program with a ValueError. A safer pattern checks first: text = input("Enter your age: "), then if text.isdigit(): age = int(text), else: print("Please enter digits only"). Tracing this through, if text is "25", isdigit() returns True and the conversion proceeds safely; if text is "twenty", isdigit() returns False and the program prints a friendly message instead of crashing.

It is worth being precise about edge cases, since these methods are stricter than they first appear. isdigit() rejects negative numbers, because the minus sign is not a digit, so "-5".isdigit() is False even though -5 is a perfectly good integer. isspace() returns True only when a string is nonempty and consists entirely of whitespace characters like spaces, tabs, or newlines, so "   ".isspace() is True but "".isspace() is False. Knowing these boundary behaviors, and testing them with a few quick examples in an interpreter, is exactly the kind of careful reasoning that keeps validation logic from silently accepting bad input it should have rejected.

isupper() and islower() are slightly different in spirit, since they check the case of letters rather than what kind of character is present at all. "HELLO".isupper() is True, "Hello".isupper() is False because not every letter is uppercase, and "123".isupper() is also False, since a string needs at least one cased letter for isupper() or islower() to return True at all. It is common to combine validation with cleanup: raw input often carries stray whitespace from the user pressing space by accident, so a realistic check looks more like if text.strip().isdigit(), which first removes leading and trailing whitespace with strip() and then tests what remains, so " 25 ".strip().isdigit() correctly evaluates to True even though " 25 ".isdigit() by itself would be False because of the surrounding spaces.
